title: Bob Dylan
why: His debut, produced by John Hammond and cut in a handful of sessions in November 1961, is mostly folk and blues standards with just two originals. It sold poorly but caught the raw energy of his early club sets.
essay: Dylan was twenty when he walked into Columbia's New York studio in late 1961, a newcomer signed by John Hammond after a few months on the Greenwich Village club circuit. The sessions were quick and cheap: just Dylan, his acoustic guitar and his harmonica, with almost no retakes. The songs came mostly from the blues and folk repertoire he had been playing nightly, and he leans hard on death and hard luck, singing in a rasping, deliberately aged voice far older than his years. Only "Talkin' New York" and "Song to Woody", his tribute to Woody Guthrie, were his own. When the album came out in 1962 it made little impression, and some at Columbia took to calling him Hammond's folly. Yet it is a vivid snapshot of a young performer still finding himself, and within months he was writing songs that would make covers unnecessary.

title: The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan
why: His second album was made almost entirely of his own songs, and it turned a promising folk interpreter into the most talked-about songwriter of his generation. It holds protest anthems, apocalyptic visions and tender love songs side by side, under the famous cover photo of Dylan and Suze Rotolo on a snowy Greenwich Village street.
essay: Dylan recorded his second album over many sessions between the spring of 1962 and the spring of 1963, first with John Hammond and then with Tom Wilson producing, and the running order changed more than once before release. Most of it is just Dylan alone with guitar and harmonica, though "Corrina, Corrina" carries a small backing band. The songs move freely between moods: furious protest, long visionary ballads, wry talking blues and gentle, rueful love songs shaped by his relationship with Suze Rotolo, who was away in Italy for much of the time. A song mocking the John Birch Society was dropped before release, reportedly over the label's legal worries. When Peter, Paul and Mary turned "Blowin' in the Wind" into a hit in 1963, Dylan's name spread far beyond the Village, and the album became a touchstone for the folk revival and for countless songwriters who followed.

title: Another Side of Bob Dylan
why: Recorded in a single night session in June 1964, it trades topical protest for personal, playful and searching songs. It marked his break from the role of folk spokesman.
essay: Dylan cut this album in New York in one long evening in June 1964, with Tom Wilson producing and friends drifting in and out of the studio. He played it almost entirely alone on guitar and harmonica, with piano on one track, and the loose, sometimes giggling performances reflect the speed of the session. Many of the songs had been written on travels earlier that year, including a stay in Europe. Gone were the newspaper-headline ballads; in their place came comic shaggy-dog stories, flirtatious love songs, a bitter account of a breakup and a few searching reflections on his own earlier certainties. Folk purists were dismayed, and parts of the folk press publicly scolded him for turning inward. Other artists heard something new, and the Byrds and the Turtles would soon find hits in its songs. Looking back, it is the hinge between the protest singer and the electric poet who arrived next.

title: The Times They Are a-Changin'
why: His first album of entirely original songs is his most starkly topical, with ballads of poverty, racist murder and unjust courts. Its title song became an anthem of the 1960s, and its closing farewell already hints that he was ready to move on.
essay: Recorded in New York in the late summer and autumn of 1963 with Tom Wilson producing, his third album is the most austere record he ever made: one voice, one guitar, a harmonica, and nothing to soften the subject matter. These are songs of the civil rights era and of hard times in small towns, several drawn from real events, including the killing of Medgar Evers and the death of Hattie Carroll in Baltimore. Alongside them sit a few personal songs about distance and parting that hint at a different writer underneath. The title track was written to be an anthem and was taken up as one almost immediately. The record arrived in early 1964, just weeks after the assassination of John F. Kennedy, and it cemented his place as the voice of protest. That was a role he was already growing restless in, and within months he would set it aside.

title: Bringing It All Back Home
why: Dylan split the record into an electric side with a rock band and an acoustic side of long, image-packed songs. It was the first album where he plugged in, and it showed his writing moving from topical protest toward surreal, personal poetry.
essay: Recorded in New York in January 1965 with Tom Wilson producing, this album took only a few sessions, with Dylan often teaching the band songs on the spot. One side features electric guitars, bass and drums, with guitarist Bruce Langhorne among the players; the other is mostly Dylan with acoustic guitar, joined by Langhorne's shimmering electric lines on "Mr. Tambourine Man". The electric songs are fast, funny and sly, drawing on Chuck Berry and the blues, while the acoustic side holds some of his longest and darkest visions of society and self. It was released in March 1965, and that summer the Byrds took "Mr. Tambourine Man" to the top of the charts, helping launch folk rock as a genre. The album drew a clear line under his protest years and set the stage for his electric set at Newport a few months later.

title: Highway 61 Revisited
why: Recorded mostly with a full electric band including Mike Bloomfield and Al Kooper, it opened with Like a Rolling Stone and closed with the eleven-minute Desolation Row. It is the album where his folk-rock sound arrived fully formed, mixing blues with sprawling, sardonic storytelling.
essay: The album began in June 1965 with "Like a Rolling Stone", produced by Tom Wilson; Bob Johnston took over for the rest of the summer sessions in New York. Mike Bloomfield's stinging blues guitar and Al Kooper's organ, which he improvised on a song he barely knew, define much of the sound, a rough, ringing mix of Chicago blues and rock and roll. Between the sessions came the Newport Folk Festival, where Dylan's electric set split his audience. The record is named after the highway that runs from his home state of Minnesota down through the Mississippi Delta, and it is full of grotesque characters, absurd scenes and biting humor. It closes with a long, mostly acoustic song, its guitar part played by Charlie McCoy. Released at the end of August 1965, it was hailed as a landmark, and many still rank it as his greatest album.

title: Blonde on Blonde
why: Cut largely in Nashville with session players and Al Kooper and Robbie Robertson, it was one of rock's first double albums. Its loose, shimmering sound and mix of love songs, blues and long reveries capped his electric period.
essay: Sessions began in New York with members of the Hawks, the group later known as the Band, but progress was slow. Early in 1966 producer Bob Johnston moved the work to Nashville, where seasoned players such as Charlie McCoy, Kenny Buttrey and Hargus Robbins joined Al Kooper and Robbie Robertson. The Nashville musicians often waited for hours while Dylan finished writing, then caught songs in a few takes, giving the record its relaxed, late-night glow. The sound is thinner and more delicate than the album before, built on organ, piano and lightly chiming guitars, and the songs range from brass-band larks to tender ballads and long, dreamy meditations, one of them filling an entire side. Released in mid-1966, it was quickly recognized as a high point of the decade. Weeks later his motorcycle accident ended the frantic electric period it crowned.

title: John Wesley Harding
why: Released in late 1967 after more than a year of silence, it swapped the wild electric sound of 1966 for spare Nashville recordings with a tiny band. Its short, biblical parables about outlaws, drifters and saints set the quiet tone for the rest of his country years.
essay: After the motorcycle accident in 1966 Dylan withdrew to Woodstock, and for more than a year the public heard nothing new. In late 1967 he went to Nashville with Bob Johnston and recorded this album over a few short sessions, backed only by Charlie McCoy on bass and Kenny Buttrey on drums, with Pete Drake's pedal steel added to the two closing songs. Compared with the swirling sound of 1966, it is startlingly bare: acoustic guitar, harmonica, a light rhythm section and short, carefully weighed verses. The songs read like parables, populated by outlaws, immigrants, saints and messengers, and they echo the Bible and American folklore he was steeped in at the time. Released just after Christmas 1967, at the height of psychedelia, it seemed to point rock music back toward simplicity. Jimi Hendrix's electrifying version of "All Along the Watchtower" the following year became the definitive one, as Dylan himself later acknowledged.

title: Nashville Skyline
why: Recorded in Nashville and released in 1969, it showed Dylan singing in a smooth croon few listeners recognized. Its brief country love songs, a duet with Johnny Cash and the hit Lay Lady Lay helped bring rock and country audiences together.
essay: Dylan returned to Nashville in early 1969 with Bob Johnston and many of the same session players, and the record was finished quickly. It is short, under half an hour, and it opens with a duet with Johnny Cash on a song from his second album, the result of sessions the two men shared during the visit. Most striking was his voice: smooth, warm and low, so unlike his earlier rasp that some listeners hardly knew it was him. The songs are simple, sunny country tunes about love and longing, with pedal steel and an easygoing pace, plus a bouncy instrumental. "Lay Lady Lay" became a hit single, and Dylan appeared on Cash's new television show that year. Some critics found the album slight, but it gave country music a new credibility among rock fans, and it helped open the road toward the country rock of the years that followed.

title: New Morning
why: Arriving only months after Self Portrait, it was welcomed as a return to original songwriting with warm, domestic songs about family and country life.
essay: Recorded in New York in 1970, with Bob Johnston credited as producer and Al Kooper closely involved, the album followed Self Portrait by only four months. Dylan plays piano on much of it, and the sound is warm and homespun, touched with gospel, country and even a dash of jazz on one track. A few songs began as music for a stage play by the poet Archibald MacLeish, a collaboration that fell apart. Another was inspired by his trip to Princeton to receive an honorary degree that year. Elsewhere he sings about contentment, the countryside and family life, the mood of a man settled with his wife and children. Critics who had been baffled by Self Portrait greeted it with relief, some hailing it as a comeback. George Harrison soon recorded "If Not for You", and the album has kept a quiet, affectionate following ever since.

title: Self Portrait
why: A 1970 double album made mostly of covers, traditional songs and a few live tracks, it baffled critics and fans expecting new Dylan songs. Later reissues of its sessions earned it a kinder reassessment.
essay: Self Portrait was assembled from sessions in Nashville and New York in 1969 and 1970, produced by Bob Johnston, along with a handful of performances from the Isle of Wight Festival in 1969, where Dylan played with the Band. It is a sprawling double album of folk standards, pop and country covers, a few instrumentals and only a handful of originals. He sings songs by Paul Simon and Gordon Lightfoot, old ballads and pop standards, often in his Nashville croon, and some tracks carry orchestral strings and backing singers added later. Many critics took it as careless or even a deliberate joke, and Greil Marcus's long review in Rolling Stone became famous for its scorn. Dylan later suggested he had partly wanted to shake off his image as a generational prophet. In 2013 the Bootleg Series released the sessions in plainer, unadorned form as Another Self Portrait, and many listeners heard the music with fresh ears.

title: Dylan
why: Columbia assembled this album of cover versions from old outtakes after Dylan left the label for Asylum, without his involvement.
essay: In 1973 Dylan's Columbia contract ran out and he signed with David Geffen's Asylum label. Columbia responded by putting together this album from leftover studio performances, mainly from the Self Portrait and New Morning sessions of 1969 and 1970, and releasing it late that year without his involvement. It is made entirely of covers: an Elvis Presley ballad, songs by Joni Mitchell and Jerry Jeff Walker, Peter La Farge's ballad about Ira Hayes, and several traditional folk songs. The performances lean on his Nashville-era croon and on backing singers, and many sound like warm-ups never meant for release. Critics widely regarded it as a low point and as a label's revenge on a departing star. Dylan returned to Columbia in 1974, and the album was long left out of print in many markets. Its tracks were eventually reissued as part of a large collection of his complete albums.

title: Pat Garrett & Billy the Kid
why: His soundtrack for Sam Peckinpah's western is mostly instrumental, but it produced one of his most widely covered songs.
essay: Dylan came to Sam Peckinpah's western through the screenwriter Rudy Wurlitzer, and he ended up not only writing the score but acting in the film, as a quiet drifter named Alias who rides with Billy the Kid. The music was recorded in Mexico City, where the film was shot, and later in California, with musicians including Roger McGuinn, Jim Keltner and Booker T. Jones. Much of the album is instrumental: loose guitar figures, mournful harmonica and themes that repeat in different shades, made to sit beneath the action. The film was cut by its studio against Peckinpah's wishes, and the soundtrack drew mixed reviews at the time. But one short song, "Knockin' on Heaven's Door", written for a death scene, became a hit and went on to be recorded by Eric Clapton, Guns N' Roses and many more. It ranks among the most covered songs he has ever written.

title: Planet Waves
why: Recorded with the Band in Los Angeles, it was his first album for Asylum and his first to reach number one in the US.
essay: Dylan had not made a full album of new songs in more than three years when he went into a Los Angeles studio in November 1973 with the Band, his old companions from 1966 and the basement sessions. The record was made fast, in a few days, with engineer Rob Fraboni, and the Band's playing is loose, rootsy and warm, built on Garth Hudson's organ and Robbie Robertson's guitar. The songs are mostly about home, love and devotion, with a few darker ones running underneath, and "Forever Young" appears in two contrasting versions, slow and fast. Dylan drew the cover art himself. Released in January 1974 on Asylum, it coincided with his first major tour in eight years, with the Band, which drew enormous demand for tickets. Critics were respectful rather than overwhelmed, and the album has tended to be overshadowed by the one that followed.

title: Blood on the Tracks
why: Written as his marriage was breaking down, these songs of love, regret and memory are often ranked among the best of his career. He recorded it in New York in September 1974, then re-cut five songs with local musicians in Minneapolis that December, and those versions made the final record.
essay: By 1974 Dylan's marriage was in trouble, and the songs he wrote that year are full of loss, anger, tenderness and memory, told with shifting points of view and time that slides back and forth. He recorded them in New York in September with a small group, the arrangements often reduced to his guitar, harmonica and a bass. Just before release, his brother David persuaded him to try some songs again in Minneapolis, where local musicians cut new versions of five of them over the holidays. Those fuller, livelier takes replaced the New York ones, giving the album its mix of intimacy and drive. It came out in January 1975 on Columbia, to which he had returned, and it was soon hailed as a masterpiece and a return to form. Dylan has played down its autobiographical side, but it remains one of the most admired breakup albums ever made.

title: The Basement Tapes
why: Columbia finally released these 1967 recordings made with the Band near Woodstock in 1975, adding some Band-only tracks to the Dylan songs that had circulated for years on bootlegs.
essay: In 1967, while Dylan recovered from his accident near Woodstock, he and the Hawks gathered almost daily to play, first at his home and then in the basement of a pink house in West Saugerties that the group shared. Garth Hudson recorded the sessions on a simple tape machine. They ran through old folk songs, country tunes and dozens of new Dylan songs, some funny and nonsensical, others haunting. Demo tapes went out to other artists, and hits followed for Manfred Mann, the Byrds and others, while bootlegs spread the music from 1969 on. When Columbia finally issued this double album in 1975, Robbie Robertson compiled it, adding tracks by the Band alone and some later overdubs. Critics welcomed it warmly, and its sound, rough, homemade and rooted in old American music, has influenced generations of musicians. The complete sessions appeared in the Bootleg Series in 2014.

title: Desire
why: Made with lyricist Jacques Levy, a violinist named Scarlet Rivera and harmony singer Emmylou Harris, it mixes long story songs with deeply personal ones. It spent five weeks at number one in the US and many of its songs were played on the Rolling Thunder Revue.
essay: Dylan wrote most of these songs in 1975 with the theatre director Jacques Levy, and the partnership pushed him toward long, cinematic stories. They were recorded in New York that summer with producer Don DeVito, after some crowded early sessions gave way to a lean group: Scarlet Rivera's violin, Rob Stoner's bass, Howie Wyeth's drums and Emmylou Harris singing harmony. The violin gives the album its sound, swirling and slightly exotic, with touches of Mexican and Middle Eastern color. "Hurricane" took up the case of the imprisoned boxer Rubin Carter, while "Joey" romanticized a murdered New York gangster and drew sharp criticism. The album closes with a direct, unguarded song addressed to his wife, Sara. Released in January 1976, it was a big commercial success, and many of its songs were already familiar to audiences of the Rolling Thunder Revue, the touring troupe he had launched that autumn.

title: Street-Legal
why: Recorded in his own Santa Monica studio with the large band from his 1978 tour, it pairs dense, symbolic songs with horns and gospel-style backing singers.
essay: After a world tour in early 1978 with a large band, Dylan took the same group into Rundown, his rehearsal studio in Santa Monica, and recorded the album in about a week with producer Don DeVito. The sound is big and soulful: saxophone, keyboards and a trio of gospel-trained women singers answering his vocals, a long way from the folk or country records of the past. The songs are dense and full of symbolic imagery, about broken relationships, spiritual searching and a sense of danger, and they foreshadow the religious turn that came soon after. The original mix was widely criticized as murky, and American critics were generally cool. In Britain it found a warmer welcome, helped by a big European tour that year. A remixed version issued in 1999 brought out the detail, and the album's reputation has risen steadily since.

title: Slow Train Coming
why: His first album after becoming a born-again Christian, it set evangelical lyrics to a polished R&B sound cut at Muscle Shoals with producers Jerry Wexler and Barry Beckett. Mark Knopfler's guitar and a Grammy-winning single made it a commercial success even as it divided longtime fans.
essay: Late in 1978 Dylan became a born-again Christian, and the songs he wrote in the following months were about faith, sin and judgment. To record them he turned to Jerry Wexler, the veteran producer of Aretha Franklin, who brought him to Muscle Shoals in Alabama in the spring of 1979 with Barry Beckett as co-producer. The band included Mark Knopfler and drummer Pick Withers of Dire Straits, along with the Muscle Shoals horns and backing singers. The result is the most polished-sounding record he had made: tight grooves, clean guitar and a confident, often fierce vocal. Released that August, it sold well, and "Gotta Serve Somebody" brought Dylan his first Grammy for a solo vocal performance. Critics and fans were split, some admiring the music and others put off by its preaching, but it opened his most controversial chapter in earnest.

title: Saved
why: A fuller gospel record, cut with his touring band and backing singers, that captures the fervor of the gospel-only concerts.
essay: Dylan returned to Muscle Shoals with Jerry Wexler and Barry Beckett in February 1980, this time with the band he had been touring with since late 1979: guitarist Fred Tackett, bassist Tim Drummond, drummer Jim Keltner, keyboard players Spooner Oldham and Terry Young, and a group of gospel singers. Those shows were made up only of his new religious songs, and the album tries to bottle their energy, though it was cut quickly and some felt it lacked the spark of the stage. It sounds rawer and more churchlike than its predecessor, with call-and-response vocals, rolling piano and organ. It opens with a country gospel song, the album's one cover. Released that summer with a painting of a reaching hand on the cover, later replaced, it sold poorly and drew lukewarm reviews. Many listeners have since rediscovered these songs through live recordings from the tours.

title: Shot of Love
why: Mixing faith songs with secular ones, it closed the gospel period and ends with Every Grain of Sand.
essay: Dylan recorded Shot of Love in Los Angeles in 1981, mostly with producer Chuck Plotkin, keeping the gospel singers and road musicians who had backed him on his recent tours. The sound is rougher and more rock-driven than the two records before it, with loud drums, ringing guitars and a choir of women's voices answering his lead. Alongside songs of belief sit things he had not done in two years: a tender tribute in "Lenny Bruce" to the comedian, and love songs such as "Heart of Mine". The closer, "Every Grain of Sand", is a quiet, searching hymn that many now count among his finest songs. At the time, though, reviews were cool and sales were weak, and some strong songs from the sessions were left off. Its reputation has grown since, and listeners now hear it as a bridge out of the gospel years.

title: Infidels
why: His first secular album after three gospel records, Infidels was co-produced with Mark Knopfler and built on the reggae rhythm section of Sly Dunbar and Robbie Shakespeare. Its songs mix politics, scripture and romance, and it was seen as a return to strong songwriting, though Dylan left some of the best material from the sessions unreleased.
essay: After three religious albums, Dylan went to the Power Station in New York in 1983 with Mark Knopfler of Dire Straits as co-producer. The band was a strong one: Sly Dunbar and Robbie Shakespeare on drums and bass, Mick Taylor and Knopfler on guitars. The result is clean and spacious, with a gentle reggae lilt under several songs and sharp guitar lines throughout. The writing ranges widely, from the shifting, dreamlike "Jokerman" to the blunt politics of "Union Sundown" and "Neighborhood Bully" and the plea of "Don't Fall Apart on Me Tonight". Knopfler left to tour before the mixing was done, and Dylan finished the record himself, reworking vocals and cutting songs. Reviewers welcomed it as a return, but fans later learned what had been dropped, above all "Blind Willie McTell", which surfaced years afterward on The Bootleg Series and is now widely seen as one of his greatest songs.

title: Empire Burlesque
why: Dylan's most polished attempt at a mid-1980s radio sound, with drum machines, horns and backing singers, ending on a solo acoustic song.
essay: Empire Burlesque was pieced together over many months of 1984 and 1985 in New York and Los Angeles, with a long and shifting list of players, including members of Tom Petty's Heartbreakers and the rhythm section of Sly Dunbar and Robbie Shakespeare. Dylan then handed the tapes to Arthur Baker, a producer known for dance remixes, who gave the mix its glossy, punchy finish. The record leans hard into the sound of mid-1980s radio, with gated drums, synthesizers, horn stabs and female backing vocals, and songs such as "Tight Connection to My Heart" were promoted with music videos. Under the sheen are romantic, sometimes witty songs that borrow freely from old films. The final track, "Dark Eyes", drops all of that for one voice, a guitar and a harmonica. Critics were divided at the time; some praised its energy, while others found the production dated it quickly. Its strongest songs have aged better than its sound.

title: Knocked Out Loaded
why: A patchwork of covers and co-writes, it is remembered mainly for the eleven-minute Brownsville Girl.
essay: Knocked Out Loaded came together in 1986 around Dylan's touring with Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, assembled from sessions old and new rather than planned as a whole. It mixes covers, gospel and country songs with co-writes: one with Petty, another with Carole Bayer Sager, and a Kris Kristofferson song sung with a children's choir. The sound swings from loose rhythm and blues to slick backing vocals, and much of it feels unfinished. At its center, though, is "Brownsville Girl", an eleven-minute song written with the playwright Sam Shepard. It began life as a different song in the Empire Burlesque sessions, and it unfolds like a road movie, drifting between a Western film, memory and a love affair, with Dylan half speaking and half singing over a full band and gospel singers. Reviews of the album were poor and sales were low, but that one song has kept a devoted following and is often named among his best.

title: Down in the Groove
why: Made up mostly of covers and leftovers, it was among the weakest-selling albums of his career.
essay: Down in the Groove was released in 1988, just before Dylan began the touring that would become known as the Never Ending Tour. It gathers covers and outtakes from several years of sessions, cut with very different casts, from Eric Clapton and Mark Knopfler to members of the Sex Pistols and the Clash. Two songs, "Silvio" and "Ugliest Girl in the World", were written with the Grateful Dead lyricist Robert Hunter, and members of the Dead sing on "Silvio", which became a regular in Dylan's concerts. The rest leans on rhythm and blues, country and folk, ending with a quiet reading of the Stanley Brothers' "Rank Strangers to Me". Because the tracks come from scattered sessions, the album has little shape, and critics treated it as a low point. Even so, his plain, worn singing on the folk and country songs points toward the traditional albums he would make a few years later.

title: Oh Mercy
why: Recorded in New Orleans with producer Daniel Lanois, Oh Mercy wrapped new songs in a dark, atmospheric sound. Critics hailed it as his strongest album in years, and Dylan later devoted a long chapter of Chronicles: Volume One to making it.
essay: Bono suggested that Dylan work with Daniel Lanois, and in early 1989 the two set up in a house in New Orleans that Lanois had turned into a studio. They worked mostly at night with a small group of local players, including Cyril Neville on percussion, and Lanois shaped a dark, humid sound of echoing guitars, low drums and close, intimate vocals. Dylan had arrived with new songs written over the previous year, and the album moves between social complaint, as in "Political World" and "Everything Is Broken", and private reckonings such as "Most of the Time" and "What Good Am I?". "Ring Them Bells" is played almost alone at the piano. The two men sometimes clashed, and songs such as "Dignity" and "Series of Dreams" were left off. Reviewers called it his best album in a decade, and Dylan's long account of the sessions in his memoir made it one of his most closely studied records.

title: Under the Red Sky
why: Produced by Don Was and David Was with guests including George Harrison, Elton John and Slash, it mixes nursery-rhyme simplicity with a rock band sound.
essay: Dylan made Under the Red Sky quickly in Los Angeles in early 1990 with the brothers Don and David Was producing, the same year he recorded with the Traveling Wilburys. A long list of famous players dropped in, among them George Harrison, Elton John, Slash, David Crosby, Bruce Hornsby and the brothers Stevie Ray and Jimmie Vaughan. The music is straightforward rock and blues, often built on short, simple riffs, and many of the songs are written like nursery rhymes or fables, with riddling characters and plain, repeating forms. The album is dedicated to a young child, which some listeners take as a key to its tone. Coming after Oh Mercy, it puzzled critics, and the opening "Wiggle Wiggle" was widely mocked. Over time more listeners have come to hear the fairy-tale songs, and the title track in particular, as deliberate and even haunting rather than careless.

title: Good as I Been to You
why: His first album of just voice, guitar and harmonica since 1964, made up entirely of traditional songs and old blues.
essay: In 1992 Dylan began an album with a band and the guitarist David Bromberg, then set those sessions aside and recorded alone in his garage studio in Malibu. What came out was Good as I Been to You, thirteen old songs played on acoustic guitar and harmonica, with no originals at all. The material ranges across British and Irish ballads such as "Arthur McBride", American murder ballads and blues, and children's songs like "Froggie Went a Courtin'". His voice is hoarse and his guitar playing busy and inventive, giving the old songs a lived-in, unpolished feel very different from the folk revival recordings of thirty years earlier. Many listeners were surprised, but critics welcomed it as a return to his roots and a sign of renewed purpose. It began a period in which old songs fed his playing and writing, and it set up the darker companion album that followed a year later.

title: World Gone Wrong
why: A second solo acoustic set of old songs, darker than the first, with Dylan's own liner notes on each track; it later won a Grammy for Best Traditional Folk Album.
essay: World Gone Wrong was recorded at home in Malibu in 1993, again with just Dylan's voice and acoustic guitar, and it went deeper into the old repertoire than its predecessor. Two songs come from the Mississippi Sheiks, one from Blind Willie McTell, and others from the long tradition of ballads about murder, war and wandering, ending with the hymn "Lone Pilgrim", which he learned from Doc Watson. The mood is heavier and the performances more stripped down, with his voice rough and close and his guitar loose and unhurried. Dylan also wrote his own liner notes, a sideways, playful essay on each song, tying it to its sources and to the troubles of the present. Critics praised its seriousness, and it won the Grammy for Best Traditional Folk Album. These two records reconnected him with the songs he had learned as a young man and prepared the ground for the original work that came later in the decade.

title: Time Out of Mind
why: Recorded with producer Daniel Lanois, it was Dylan's first album of new original songs in seven years and his first major critical comeback in decades. Its dark, aging voice and murky sound won the Grammy for Album of the Year and opened his late-career run.
essay: Dylan reunited with Daniel Lanois for Time Out of Mind, recording in Miami in early 1997 with a large band that included Jim Dickinson and Augie Meyers on keyboards, several guitarists and two drummers. The sessions were tense, as the two men again disagreed about sound, but the result is a murky, layered record in which Dylan's voice, now cracked and weathered, sits inside echoing guitars, organ and loose blues grooves. The songs keep returning to aging, lost love, distance and endurance, from the slow "Not Dark Yet" to the sixteen-minute closing ramble "Highlands". Shortly after the recording Dylan was hospitalized with a serious heart infection, and when the album came out that autumn many heard it through that news. Reviews were rapturous, and it won the Grammy for Album of the Year. "Make You Feel My Love" went on to be widely covered, and the record began the late period many count among his best.

title: "Love and Theft"
why: Released on September 11, 2001, it set Dylan's songs inside the sounds of prewar America: blues, rockabilly, swing and Tin Pan Alley. He produced it himself under the name Jack Frost with his touring band, and its title in quotation marks nods to a scholarly book on blackface minstrelsy.
essay: Dylan recorded "Love and Theft" in New York in 2001 with his touring band of the time, including guitarists Larry Campbell and Charlie Sexton, bassist Tony Garnier and drummer David Kemper, along with Augie Meyers on keyboards. He produced it himself under the name Jack Frost, and the sessions were quick and relaxed. The music moves freely through older American styles: jump blues, rockabilly, swing, parlor ballads and crooner numbers, played with the ease of a band that knew him well. Dylan sings with wit and menace, and the songs are packed with borrowed lines and characters from old records, films and books, a habit that drew both admiration and debate. "Mississippi", left off Time Out of Mind, appears here in a warm new version. The album came out on the day of the September 11 attacks, yet critics embraced it, and it won the Grammy for Best Contemporary Folk Album.

title: Modern Times
why: It entered the Billboard 200 at number one, Dylan's first chart-topping album in America since Desire in 1976. Recorded with his road band and produced by Dylan as Jack Frost, it reworked old blues and ballad forms and won the Grammy for Best Contemporary Folk/Americana Album.
essay: Modern Times was recorded in New York early in 2006 with the band Dylan had been touring with, including Denny Freeman and Stu Kimball on guitars, Donnie Herron on steel guitar and violin, George Recile on drums and Tony Garnier on bass. Dylan again produced it as Jack Frost, and he spoke of wanting the record to capture how the band sounded live. The songs lean on older forms: Chicago-style blues shuffles, soft ballads built on prewar pop melodies, and long, slow numbers such as the closing "Ain't Talkin'". As on the record before it, he drew on older sources, and observers noticed lines echoing a Civil War-era poet, which renewed debate about borrowing. The album reached number one in America, his first in thirty years. It won a Grammy, and "Someday Baby" took another, for best solo rock vocal performance.

title: Christmas in the Heart
why: A collection of holiday standards sung with full sincerity, it surprised many listeners. Dylan gave all his royalties from it to charities fighting hunger.
essay: Christmas in the Heart came out in 2009, made with his touring musicians and guests including David Hidalgo of Los Lobos. It is a full holiday record of carols, pop standards and novelty songs, arranged in the warm style of the 1950s and early 1960s, with backing choirs, steel guitar and accordion. Dylan sings in his rough late voice, which made the earnest arrangements sound strange to some ears, and "Must Be Santa" became a rowdy polka with a comic video. Many wondered whether it was a joke. In interviews Dylan said plainly that it was not, and that he sang the songs as a believer and a fan of the music. Reaction ranged from delight to bafflement. All of his royalties went to hunger charities, including Feeding America in the United States, Crisis in Britain and the United Nations World Food Programme, which gave it an appeal beyond the music itself.

title: Together Through Life
why: Written mostly with Robert Hunter and colored by David Hidalgo's accordion, it has a loose, border-town feel. It entered the charts at number one in both the US and UK.
essay: Together Through Life began when the French director Olivier Dahan asked Dylan for a song for a film, and that one song grew into an album recorded quickly in late 2008. Dylan wrote almost all of it with Robert Hunter, the Grateful Dead lyricist he had worked with before. The sound comes from Chicago blues and the music of the Texas-Mexico border: shuffling rhythms, a low twanging guitar from Mike Campbell, and above all David Hidalgo's accordion, which colors nearly every song. The mood is relaxed and often playful, with love songs, road songs and wry complaints rather than the grand statements of his previous records, and his voice is at its most gravelly. One song borrows heavily from a Willie Dixon blues, and Dixon is credited. Reviewers generally liked it as a loose, easygoing side step, and it reached number one in both the US and the UK.

title: Tempest
why: Released in the fiftieth anniversary year of his first album, it is one of his darkest records, full of violent ballads and blues. Its long title song about the Titanic and its farewell to John Lennon stand out.
essay: Tempest was recorded in 2012 at Jackson Browne's studio in Santa Monica with Dylan's touring band and David Hidalgo, and Dylan again produced it as Jack Frost. It opens gently with "Duquesne Whistle", a jaunty swing number written with Robert Hunter, but much of what follows is dark: slow, grinding blues and long story-ballads in which betrayal and violence pile up. The title song runs about fourteen minutes and tells of the sinking of the Titanic in many verses over a lilting waltz, mixing historical figures with invented ones. The album closes with "Roll on John", a tribute to John Lennon built from echoes of Beatles songs. Dylan's voice is at its harshest here, and he uses it to growl and to tease. Critics praised its ambition and its storytelling, and it came out in the fiftieth anniversary year of his first album, which many reviews noted.

title: Shadows in the Night
why: Dylan's first album of standards strips songs Frank Sinatra once recorded down to his small touring band, recorded live in the studio.
essay: For Shadows in the Night, Dylan took ten songs that Frank Sinatra had recorded and cut them at Capitol Studios in Hollywood, where Sinatra had made many of his records. Rather than copy the big orchestral arrangements, he scaled them down for his own five-piece band, with Donnie Herron's pedal steel carrying the lines once played by strings, and a few horns on some tracks. The musicians played together live around a small number of microphones, with engineer Al Schmitt capturing them with little or no overdubbing. The result is hushed and slow, and Dylan sings with surprising care and steadiness, staying close to the melodies. He said he saw the project not as covering Sinatra but as uncovering the songs. Many critics were moved by it, and he gave away copies to readers of a magazine for older Americans. It began the run of standards albums that filled the next three years.

title: Fallen Angels
why: A second set of Sinatra-associated standards, cut with the same touring band and a slightly lighter, more romantic mood.
essay: Fallen Angels was recorded at Capitol Studios with the same small touring band and engineer Al Schmitt as Shadows in the Night, and it came out in 2016, shortly before Dylan turned seventy-five. Again the songs are ones Frank Sinatra had sung, but the choice is wider and the mood is lighter, with more swing and more songs of romance and longing alongside the ballads. The arrangements stay spare: steel guitar, soft electric guitars, upright bass and brushed drums, with an occasional horn. Dylan's singing is relaxed and assured, and he clearly enjoys phrasing these melodies. Reviewers found it warmer and more varied than its predecessor, though some wondered how long he would stay in this territory. It confirmed that the standards project was more than a one-off experiment, and later that year he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, before returning to the same studio for a much larger set.

title: Triplicate
why: His first triple album, thirty standards in three themed sets of ten, closing out his run of American songbook records.
essay: Triplicate came out in 2017, the year after Dylan was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, and was his first three-disc album of new recordings. He recorded it at Capitol Studios in Hollywood with his touring band, this time with more horns in the arrangements, and arranged the thirty songs into three discs of ten, each given its own title and loosely following a mood. Some of the songs had been recorded by Frank Sinatra, while others reach wider across the American songbook, including "Stormy Weather" and "As Time Goes By". The playing is again gentle and unhurried, and Dylan's voice is patient and close, though the sheer length makes the record more of a long late-night program than a statement. Reviewers admired the care and craft but many felt the project had run its course. It was the last of his standards albums before he returned to writing his own songs.

title: Rough and Rowdy Ways
why: His first album of new original songs since Tempest in 2012, made largely of long, unhurried meditations on history, mortality and himself. It closes with the seventeen-minute "Murder Most Foul" on a disc of its own. The album went to number one in the UK.
essay: Rough and Rowdy Ways arrived in June 2020, in the early months of the pandemic. Before it, Dylan released "Murder Most Foul", a long, slow meditation on the killing of John F. Kennedy and the American culture that followed it, which became his first song to top a Billboard chart. The album was made with his touring band and guests including the guitarist and producer Blake Mills. Its sound is quiet and spacious, moving between murmured ballads, heavy blues and slow, hymn-like pieces, with Dylan's voice close and calm. The songs range over history, myth, death, love and his own legend, packed with references to writers, musicians and films. "Key West (Philosopher Pirate)" drifts for nearly ten minutes, and "Murder Most Foul" fills a disc of its own. Critics greeted it as one of the great albums of his late career, and it showed he was still writing at full strength at seventy-nine.
